note: Threat model and risk register for Hermes OS, derived entirely from the committed S0 documents and the Phase 99 register on the source state named above. Severity is computed from the declared factors by scripts/security/s1/risk-register-check.mjs; there is no manual override. Contains no secret, no request data, no timestamp and no absolute path. scoringMethod.rounding: Math.round — a half rounds up; a mean of four 0..5 integers is x.0/x.25/x.5/x.75
scoringMethod.factorOrientation: every factor 0..5, higher always means more risk; privilegeAccessibility=5 means none needed
scoringMethod.clamp: CRITICAL_REQUIRES_ACTIVE_CONFIRMED — a risk whose productionState is not ACTIVE_CONFIRMED is clamped from CRITICAL to HIGH
scoringMethod.manualOverrides: none exist; severity is always the computed value

risks.title: The legacy session HMAC key has no production guard, so a forged cookie can select any role
guardEvidence: AUTH_SECRET is set in the running web container — owner-supplied read-only presence check, recorded in EDGE-ORIGIN-AND-CLIENT-IP.md §3 together with its verdict L5_ACTIVE_IN_CURRENT_CONTAINER: NO.
Because the variable is non-empty, the published fallback constant in the signing helper is not the key in use, so forgery from that constant is not available in the observed configuration.

runtimeEvidence.statement: AUTH_SECRET is present and non-empty in the running web container.
runtimeEvidence.source: docs/security/EDGE-ORIGIN-AND-CLIENT-IP.md §3 — owner-supplied, read-only, count only; no secret value was read, compared, hashed or displayed
runtimeEvidence.proves: The hardcoded fallback is not active in the current container, so cookie forgery from the published constant is not available as the platform now runs.
doesNotProve: its independence from the other three variable names the boot check accepts
that every replica holds the same value
that it is rotated, or when it was created
that the value was never previously disclosed
that it will still be set after the next deploy

preconditions: AUTH_SECRET would have to be absent from the production container. It is present in the observed container, so the exposure is held shut by configuration rather than by code.
A deploy that omits the variable removes that guard, and nothing at startup would refuse the boot.
The attacker knows the fallback constant, which is published in this repository.

evidence.note: The four facts of the chain, each verified on the source state.
Keys off AUTH_SECRET alone and falls back to a constant with no NODE_ENV guard, unlike jwtSecret().

The two FATAL checks evaluate jwtSecret(), which accepts four variable names, so a deployment setting only JWT_SECRET passes both; the one check naming the constant is a WARNING and fires only when AUTH_SECRET is explicitly set to it.

existingControls: The variable is set in the observed container, which is what currently holds this shut — a configuration property, not a code property.
verifySession enforces an absolute 30-day ceiling on the payload's iat, so a forged token is bounded rather than eternal.
jwtSecret() does throw in production, so the access-token path is guarded even though this one is not.
controlGaps: No FATAL startup check covers AUTH_SECRET itself.
The guard the platform relies on evaluates a different resolution order from the primitive that consumes the key.
Combined with R-02, a forged payload may omit sid and is then never revocation-checked.

severityClamp.reason: observed inactive configuration in current container

acceptanceCriteria: A FATAL startup check refuses to boot in production when the legacy signing variable is absent or equal to the published fallback constant, which moves the guard out of configuration and into code.
The fallback constant is removed from the production code path, or made reachable only when NODE_ENV is not production, matching jwtSecret().
A test asserts that signSession and verifySession cannot be reached in production without an explicit AUTH_SECRET.
risks.residualRisk: The structural defect survives the favourable configuration: the boot-time guard the platform relies on evaluates a different resolution order from the primitive that consumes this key, so nothing stops a future deploy from omitting the variable. A presence check establishes presence and nothing else — strength, entropy, independence from the other accepted names, replica consistency, rotation and whether the value was ever disclosed all lie outside it, and none of them is claimed here.
risks.evidenceReconciliation: Reachability stays 1 and the score stays 20. Before the reconciliation, 1 stood for a precondition nobody had checked; it now stands for a precondition MEASURED not to hold, reachable only through a configuration or deployment change. The number is unchanged and its basis is stronger, so no factor was moved in order to move a severity.

risks.title: A session token without a sid bypasses the canonical revocation check, with no mode guard on the read side
guardEvidence: The storage mode is database in the observed deployment — owner-supplied read-only evidence, recorded in AUTH-TOKEN-LIFECYCLE.md §3.2 — and in that mode the single mint site cannot produce a sid-less credential: it throws and the caller answers a service-unavailable status with no cookies set.
AUTH_SECRET is set in the observed container (R-01's guard), so the other route to a sid-less token — forging one with the published fallback constant — is not available either.

runtimeEvidence.statement: The deployment runs storage mode database, and the legacy signing variable is set.
runtimeEvidence.source: docs/security/AUTH-TOKEN-LIFECYCLE.md §3.2 for the storage mode; docs/security/EDGE-ORIGIN-AND-CLIENT-IP.md §3 for the signing variable — both owner-supplied and read-only
runtimeEvidence.proves: Neither route to a sid-less token is open in the observed configuration, so the read-side bypass has nothing to accept.
doesNotProve: that no sid-less cookie exists in the field, which would require inspecting real cookies
that the configuration will be the same after the next recreate, redeploy or restart
anything about the signing key's strength, independence, replica consistency or rotation

preconditions: A sid-less token must exist. Both routes to one are closed by the observed configuration: database mode makes the mint site refuse rather than issue one, and the signing variable being set removes forgery from the published constant.
The risk is therefore realised only after a configuration change (R-03) or a future deploy that drops the signing variable (R-01), never through the mint path as it now runs.

evidence.note: The same check gates the middleware page gate, roughly 130 API routes, the organization actor resolver, the ERP tenant resolver and the compliance download path.
A payload with no sid is treated as active unconditionally, with no database hit and no storage-mode guard.

existingControls: The observed storage mode is database, so the mint side is active and strong: the session identifier is guaranteed non-null or the request fails closed with no cookies.
verifySession's 30-day absolute iat ceiling bounds any such token.
Logout clears all three cookies even when the server-side revoke throws.
controlGaps: The protection is entirely on the mint side; one future code path that signs a payload without a sid reopens the bypass and no read-side test would fail.
Within the 30-day window such a token is immune to logout, admin suspension and password reset.

severityClamp.reason: observed inactive configuration in current container

acceptanceCriteria: isPayloadSessionActive returns false for a sid-less payload whenever the storage mode is database, leaving session-mode behaviour unchanged.
A test asserts that a sid-less payload is refused in database mode and accepted in session mode.
A test asserts that signSession cannot be called without a sid in database mode.
risks.residualRisk: The guard is configuration, not code: session mode still accepts sid-less tokens by design, so a mode change on the next restart reopens the bypass (R-03), and a deploy dropping the signing variable reopens the forgery route (R-01). Whether any sid-less cookie is live in the field was not determined — the code bounds that question to the 30-day ceiling rather than answering it, and answering it would require inspecting real cookies, which no phase of this programme does.
risks.evidenceReconciliation: Reachability stays 1 for the same reason as R-01: the value already stood for a path gated by a condition that does not hold, and the reconciliation replaced an unchecked basis with a measured one. No factor was moved in order to move a severity.

risks.title: A storage-mode change is a deferred authentication downgrade that the next restart activates
preconditions: HERMES_STORAGE_MODE is set to session, or DATABASE_URL is removed, in the host environment.
The container is then recreated, redeployed or restarted — a running container is unaffected because the process reads its environment once.

evidence.note: After the change, logins begin issuing sid-less unrevocable cookies valid up to 30 days.
Session mode in production is noticed as a WARNING, so the process still boots.
An explicit override, then the presence of DATABASE_URL, then session.

existingControls: W7 does detect the condition and reports it.
Production is owner-verified as running database mode on the current deployment.
controlGaps: A warning does not prevent a boot, so a storage-engine change silently becomes an enforcement change.
The same root cause drives the silent repository fallback in R-32.
acceptanceCriteria: W7 becomes FATAL: a production process refuses to start in session mode.
A test asserts the refusal, and asserts that non-production environments still boot in session mode.
risks.residualRisk: A FATAL check converts a silent downgrade into an outage, which is the correct trade for an authentication control but must be stated: a mistaken environment edit will then stop the platform rather than weaken it.

risks.title: No account-level multi-factor authentication exists, so a valid credential is sufficient everywhere
preconditions: The attacker already holds a valid credential, obtained outside the platform — by reuse, phishing or a third-party breach.

evidence.note: A search for webauthn, passkey, totp and authenticator app across the application returns only a candidate application-withdrawal one-time code.
A re-authentication and step-up module exists; its scope and coverage were not established in S0.

existingControls: The authentication rate limiter is fail-closed, action-isolated and audited, which raises the cost of online guessing.
Sessions are server-authoritative and revocable for every sid-bearing token.
Public self-registration is disabled, so accounts are created only by invitation or by an administrator.
controlGaps: No second factor on login, on privilege elevation, or on any of the 13 OWNER-only operations.
No step-up requirement is demonstrated on the compliance approval and erasure-execution paths.
acceptanceCriteria: A second factor exists for interactive login and can be required per organization.
Step-up re-authentication is required for every OWNER-only operation and for role changes, with a test per operation.
The absence or presence of a second factor is recorded on the session and visible in the audit trail.
risks.residualRisk: A second factor does not protect the standing environment-driven seed account (R-05) unless that path is covered too, and it does not reach the gateway or worker credentials, which are not interactive identities.

risks.title: A standing environment-driven privileged account exists whenever two variables are present
preconditions: ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD are present in the production environment. Whether they are was not checked in S0 and no value was read.

evidence.note: Recorded as a standing env-driven privileged account.
A seed administrator is configured from the environment.

existingControls: The account is only present when both variables are set.
The authentication limiter applies to it like any other identity.
controlGaps: A long-lived credential in an environment file has no rotation, no expiry and no second factor.
Its use is not distinguished in the audit trail from any other administrator.
acceptanceCriteria: An owner read-only production check records whether the two variables are set, as counts only and never a value.
If present, the seed path is restricted to first boot, the credential is rotated, and its use is audited distinctly.
risks.residualRisk: The precondition is unverified, so this risk's state may move in either direction once the presence check is run.

risks.title: Two password-hashing libraries are present and the authoritative verifier is unestablished
preconditions: None for the gap itself: it is an absence of evidence about which verifier runs.

evidence.note: Both argon2 and bcryptjs are in the dependency set; which is authoritative, and whether a bcrypt verification path remains reachable, was not established.
A password policy module exists.

existingControls: An argon2 wrapper exists and a password policy module exists.
controlGaps: A reachable legacy verifier would set the effective strength of every stored credential, and no evidence establishes whether one is reachable.
No test asserts which algorithm new passwords use.
acceptanceCriteria: The authoritative hashing algorithm for new passwords is named in a test.
Any legacy verification path is either removed or proven to re-hash on successful verification, with a test.
risks.residualRisk: Until the verifier is established, the strength of stored credentials is unknown rather than weak; this entry records the ignorance, not a defect.

risks.title: Public candidate registration is an account-existence oracle
preconditions: None: the route is public by design and the oracle is its documented response.

evidence.note: The platform's stated posture elsewhere is that a response never confirms or denies whether an address has an account.
Answers 409 with a message naming the cause.

existingControls: A registered per-IP rate limiter is applied before any parse or write.
The sibling access-request, forgot-password and accept-invite routes are all invariant and do not enumerate.
controlGaps: This one route contradicts the posture the other four implement.
acceptanceCriteria: The route's response is invariant for an existing and a non-existing address.
A test asserts the two responses are identical, including status and body.
risks.residualRisk: Timing differences can still distinguish the two paths; closing that requires equalising the work done, which this acceptance criterion does not demand.

risks.title: Six module data layers query the database with no organization predicate
preconditions: A route must reach one of those layers with an identifier the caller does not own. Which six layers they are, and whether any route does so, is not established.

evidence.note: The lexical route inventory reports 100 per cent tenant coverage and cannot see inside a data layer, so both statements are true at once and the inventory must never be cited as isolation evidence.
States as established fact that six module data layers query Prisma with no organizationId predicate although every root model declares the column.

existingControls: Every tenant route derives the organization from the actor, and no tenant route accepts an organizationId from the client.
The tenant contract makes a query without an established tenant unwritable by type.
No cross-tenant read has been demonstrated in any phase of this programme.
controlGaps: There is no database-level backstop: no row-level security (R-09).
The six layers are not identified anywhere, so there is no list to test against.
The assurance instrument that reports coverage is structurally unable to see the gap.
acceptanceCriteria: The six layers are enumerated by name in a committed artifact, derived mechanically rather than from memory.
Each one either gains an organization predicate at the query level or is proven unreachable with a foreign identifier, with a test per layer.
A deterministic gate fails when a data-layer query against a root model carries no tenant predicate.
risks.residualRisk: A per-query gate is lexical in the same way the Phase 99 classifier is; without row-level security a future layer can still be written without a predicate and pass review.

risks.title: There is no database-level tenant backstop: filtering is entirely caller-side
preconditions: A caller-side predicate must be missing or wrong for the absence of a backstop to matter — which is exactly R-08.

evidence.note: Tenant filtering is caller-side predicates; no PostgreSQL row-level security policy was found.

The composite foreign key into the customer table uses the nullable ErpProject.organizationId; a composite key is not checked when a column is null, so the migration's statement that cross-tenant links are impossible in the database holds only for rows that have an organization.
275 models with 580 organizationId references, and no row-level-security policy anywhere.

existingControls: One connection string, no published database port, internal network only.
The tenant contract and the organization actor guards concentrate most predicate construction.
controlGaps: Every tenant boundary is one forgotten where clause away from being crossed, with nothing below it to refuse.
The migration role and the runtime role are the same identity (R-47), so a row-level policy could not currently be enforced against the application role alone.
The newest database-level backstop (the composite foreign key to a customer) does not bind a project row whose organization is null.
acceptanceCriteria: A decision is recorded on whether row-level security is adopted, with the reasoning, because adopting it changes every query path.
If adopted, the runtime role is separated from the migration role first (R-47), a policy exists on each root model, and a rehearsal proves a query without a tenant context returns zero rows.
If not adopted, a compensating deterministic gate is named and implemented (R-08) and the acceptance of the residual is recorded with an expiry.
risks.residualRisk: Row-level security protects rows, not aggregates computed in the application, and it cannot help where the application legitimately holds a cross-tenant role such as the platform-administrative surface.

risks.title: Site-level authorization is structurally thin, and one site-filter bypass is latent
guardEvidence: The industrial graph loader returns null on the identical condition that skips the site filter, so the filterless query has nothing to disclose — a code-path guard traced in GETPRISMA-FAILURE-CLASSIFICATION.md §13.1, not a configuration one.
The organization predicate is applied unconditionally on the same query, so cross-tenant exposure is impossible even when the site filter is skipped.
preconditions: For the latent bypass: the industrial graph loader must gain a cache, snapshot or in-process fallback. Today it returns null on the identical condition, so the skipped filter has nothing to disclose.
For the thinness: a route must handle site-scoped data without a site guard.

evidence.note: Only 9 of 410 API route files reference a site-level guard, and the schema carries 54 siteId references against 580 organizationId references.
The site filter is skipped when the client is null; cross-tenant exposure is impossible because the organization is filtered unconditionally.
The site allow-list resolver; an empty list is correctly fail-closed here.

existingControls: Site allow-list resolution is fail-closed: no accessible site means no rows.
Phase 99 fixed four separate site allow-list bypasses, so the class is known and has been remediated before.
The graph loader currently refuses on the same condition that skips the filter.
controlGaps: The site-filter construction yields undefined rather than an empty allow-list, so it fails open by shape and is masked only by a neighbour.
Site membership cannot be read or managed through the product at all (R-42), so the control has no administrative surface.
acceptanceCriteria: The site-filter construction produces an empty allow-list rather than undefined when the allow-list cannot be resolved, with a test that asserts zero rows.
Every handler that reads or writes site-scoped data is enumerated and either carries a site guard or is recorded as deliberately organization-scoped.
A negative test per site-scoped handler asserts that a member without the site is refused.
risks.residualRisk: The enumeration depends on knowing which data is site-scoped, and with 54 siteId references against 275 models that judgement is itself a design question rather than a measurement.

risks.title: Ambiguous organization membership is resolved by silently picking the oldest
preconditions: A user must be an active member of two or more organizations and reach the billing resolver without an explicit organization.

evidence.note: Resolves an unnamed organization with findFirst ordered by creation time.
Records the behaviour, and contrasts it with the contract's own refusal to carry an organization in the ambiguous state.

existingControls: The tenant contract refuses rather than guesses: its multiple-active-organizations state carries no organization identifier, and the compliance scope helper answers 409 in that case.
controlGaps: The billing resolver does not follow the contract's refusal, so one subsystem guesses where the rest refuse.
acceptanceCriteria: The billing resolver refuses when membership is ambiguous, matching the tenant contract, and a test asserts the refusal for a two-organization member.
risks.residualRisk: Refusing changes behaviour for existing multi-organization users, so the change needs a product decision about how such a user selects an organization for billing.

risks.title: Redis keys carry no namespace, and tenant scoping of cache keys is unverified
preconditions: Two tenant-scoped values would have to collide on one key for a cache bleed; whether any key omits the organization is not established.

evidence.note: Key construction is entirely caller-side.
The same caller-side pattern.
No global key prefix or namespace is configured.

existingControls: Redis is not published on a host port and requires a password.
The rate limiter degrades to an in-process window rather than to no limit.
controlGaps: There is no mechanism that forces a tenant-scoped key to embed the organization, so correctness rests on each call site.
A flat colon-delimited namespace shared by six subsystems has no collision guard.
acceptanceCriteria: Every Redis key builder is enumerated by a deterministic gate that fails the build on an unclassified one, and each is classified as tenant-scoped or global.
Tenant-scoped keys are produced by a helper that cannot omit the organization, and a test asserts that two organizations cannot collide.
risks.residualRisk: A key-builder helper does not retrofit keys already written; a namespace change needs a migration or an acceptable cache-miss window.

risks.title: The privilege-reporting instrument cannot represent the privilege model it reports on
preconditions: None: the gap is in the instrument, and 59 privileged operations were found to be correctly enforced at the API.

evidence.note: 59 privileged operations are false negatives: 9 owner-only and 50 tenant-admin, plus one whole enforcement mechanism with no textual signature.
The two privileged classifications are reported as zero on the current source state.
Eight emittable classifications, three scopes, and no code path that can emit the two privileged ones.

existingControls: No false positives were found: every classification examined was correct or under-stated.
An undeclared surface with no evidence fails to unknown rather than to a permissive default, and unknown fails readiness.
Comments are stripped before matching, so a commented-out guard does not count.
controlGaps: A reader or a gate that treats the two zeros as a measurement is misled, and Gate C and the Phase 99 assurance reports consume this output.
The unit of counting is the handler, while the privilege boundary is per action.
The token table is hand-maintained with no tie to the helpers it tracks, and carries a dead token.
acceptanceCriteria: The two privileged classifications either become emittable or are removed from the schema, so no zero can be read as a measurement.
The classifier reads the permission argument and joins it against the permission table to derive the tier mechanically.
The unit of counting becomes path, method and action, resolving action-permission maps and ternaries.
Guard helpers are registered by module provenance so a rename fails the gate, and the dead token is removed.
Capability booleans such as the compensation capability can declare themselves, with the compensation boundary as the first registered example.
risks.residualRisk: A static classifier can be made accurate about declared guards and still cannot prove a guard is reached on every branch; that limit survives any rebuild and must stay stated wherever the output is cited.

risks.title: Per-tier negative authorization tests were not assessable, so refusal is argued rather than executed
preconditions: None: the gap is the absence of executed evidence.

evidence.note: The negative-control review is static reasoning over each call chain, which is sound evidence of a different kind from an executed refusal.
The two targeted classifier tests could not be executed because the security worktree has no installed dependencies, and not executed means not reported as passing.

existingControls: Every privileged call chain examined was traced to its decision point and found correctly enforced.
The three places that accept a client-supplied role all clamp it, and the clamp is a recorded fix for a real prior defect.
controlGaps: For 59 privileged operations there is no executed assertion that a role one step below the requirement is refused.
acceptanceCriteria: For each of the 59 privileged operations a test asserts that the role one step below the requirement receives the expected refusal status.
The two existing targeted classifier tests are executed in an environment where they can run, and their result is reported.
The suite runs in continuous integration so a new privileged operation without a negative test fails the build.
risks.residualRisk: A negative test per operation proves refusal for the roles it enumerates; a new role or a new action inside an existing handler is not covered until the matrix is extended.

risks.title: Four organization-governance questions are undecided, including whether an organization can lose its only owner
preconditions: For the last-owner question: an administrator must remove the sole owner. It was not demonstrated as reachable, and it needs a policy answer before a test.

evidence.note: The four ambiguities, each needing a decision rather than a measurement.
Member removal is an owner-or-admin permission.
13 owner-only and 15 owner-or-admin permissions; no role can assign owner.

existingControls: No role can assign the owner role by any route, which is a deliberate and load-bearing clamp.
Ownership transfer is not exposed, so it cannot be abused.
The compensation capability is enforced in the repository layer, not only in the client.
controlGaps: An organization that loses its owner has no holder of 13 permissions and no API path to regain one.
Two sources of truth govern the compensation rule.
A permission table containing entries no route consults invites a false sense of coverage.
acceptanceCriteria: The owner records a decision on each of the four questions: owner immutability, the last-owner invariant, which source of truth governs the compensation rule, and whether organization deletion should exist.
Each decision is then expressed as a test or as a recorded acceptance, and the permission table is reconciled with the decisions.
risks.residualRisk: Until the decisions are recorded, an administrator action that leaves an organization without an owner is neither prevented nor known to be reachable.

risks.title: The IP pseudonymisation salt can be silently absent, turning a privacy control into a reversible hash
guardEvidence: JWT_ACCESS_SECRET is set in the observed container — owner-supplied read-only presence check, recorded in PUBLIC-ROUTE-INVENTORY.md §3.1 under the H-1 production status, which states the finding is LATENT and not active in production.
The media view beacon already fails closed on an absent salt and stores nothing, so one of the three call sites is guarded by code rather than by configuration.

runtimeEvidence.statement: JWT_ACCESS_SECRET is present and non-empty in the running web container.
runtimeEvidence.source: docs/security/PUBLIC-ROUTE-INVENTORY.md §3.1 — owner-supplied, read-only presence check; no secret value was read or displayed
runtimeEvidence.proves: The salt is non-empty in the observed container, so no unsalted pseudonym is being written as the platform now runs.
doesNotProve: its independence from the signing key
value stability across replicas and deploys
that the construction is a keyed message authentication code rather than a plain hash
that the address being hashed is the visitor's rather than an edge node's

preconditions: A deployment would have to set only JWT_SECRET, leaving JWT_ACCESS_SECRET undefined, after which the salt becomes the literal string undefined.
The variable is set in the observed container, so the exposure is held shut by configuration rather than by code.

evidence.note: The repository already understands the threat: the media view beacon guards exactly this and states that an unsalted hash of a 32-bit address space is reversible by brute force in seconds.
Hashes the address concatenated with an environment variable, with no check that the variable exists.
The identical unguarded construction.
Accepts four variable names, so a deployment can authenticate correctly while this one variable is undefined.

existingControls: The media view beacon hashes only when a salt exists and stores null otherwise — the correct posture, already implemented once.
The owner-verified presence check establishes that the variable is set on the current container.
controlGaps: Two of three call sites have no guard, so the control depends on a variable name that the authentication path does not require.
The construction is a plain hash of address plus secret rather than a keyed message authentication code, with no key version and no rotation path.
Combined with R-26, the hashed value is a Cloudflare edge address rather than the visitor's, so the pseudonym is also useless for its stated purpose.
acceptanceCriteria: A dedicated key for address pseudonymisation exists, independent of any signing key, and is read through one helper.
All three call sites fail closed when the key is absent, storing null rather than an unsalted hash, with a test per site.
The construction is a keyed message authentication code carrying a key version, and a rotation and migration policy is recorded.
A bounded retention period for the stored pseudonyms is recorded.
risks.residualRisk: The S0 public-route inventory recorded a provisional severity of MEDIUM for this finding before S1 owned the rating; the declared method places it HIGH because exploitability is near-total once the precondition holds. Both readings are in the register: the productionState records that it is not active today.

risks.title: Six unauthenticated endpoints publish an internal commercial dashboard built from fabricated records
preconditions: None: the six handlers are reachable anonymously as the platform stands.

evidence.note: Classified MISCLASSIFIED_PROTECTED for two independent reasons: a customer-success book of business is not public by design, and publishing invented commercial relationships naming real companies is a misrepresentation risk independent of any security question.
No authentication, authorization, rate limiting or audit.
Static fixture records rather than a database query; the module reaches no database at all.

existingControls: Because the module touches no database, there is no tenant data behind the routes today and therefore no cross-tenant leakage.
controlGaps: The authorization gap exists now, before the real data arrives; whatever replaces the fixtures will be tenant data and the route would then be an unauthenticated tenant-data endpoint.
Project guidance forbids fake data on production paths, and these endpoints publish invented commercial relationships with named real companies.
The customer-relationship data model carries no organization column, so there is no tenant predicate available to add.
acceptanceCriteria: The six handlers are either removed or placed behind the same gate as every other tenant surface, before any real data is wired to them.
A test asserts an anonymous request is refused.
If the surface is kept, the data model gains a tenant column and a predicate, and the fixtures are removed from the production path.
risks.residualRisk: THE SEVERITY OF THIS ENTRY CHANGES CLASS THE DAY THE FIXTURES ARE REPLACED. Today the impact is reputational and architectural because no real data is behind it; with real customer data and no tenant predicate it becomes an unauthenticated cross-tenant disclosure and this register must be re-scored before that change ships.

risks.title: Public certificate verification returns a named individual with no rate limit and unprovable token entropy
preconditions: For enumeration to be feasible the verification token must be short, sequential or otherwise low-entropy. That cannot be established from this repository because nothing in the application writes the token — there is no mint site here.

evidence.note: Verdict BLOCKED_BY_POLICY_AMBIGUITY: a 128-bit random token makes this safe, a sequential or short value makes it a personal-data enumeration surface, and there is no rate limit to slow guessing either way.
Public verification by token, returning certificate metadata and the holder's real name resolved from the user table, with no rate limit.

existingControls: Phase 99 fixed the verdict itself so an expired certificate no longer verifies as valid with the holder's name attached.
The token is the capability, which is a reasonable design for a verification endpoint.
controlGaps: No rate limit on a public endpoint that returns a named individual.
The token generator is outside this repository, so its entropy is not reviewable here.
acceptanceCriteria: The issuance path and its token generator are located and recorded; if issuance happens outside this repository, that is itself the answer and is recorded as such.
The token is proven to carry at least 128 bits of cryptographically random entropy, or it is replaced.
A registered rate limit is applied to the verification endpoint, with a test.
risks.residualRisk: Until the generator is located the enumeration risk is unrated rather than low. A rate limit bounds guessing but does not make a low-entropy token acceptable for an endpoint that returns a person's name.

risks.title: Public writers have no idempotency, and one enforces its rate limit per process rather than per cluster
preconditions: None: both routes are public by design and the behaviour is their current implementation.

evidence.note: One row created per submission with no idempotency or duplicate suppression.
A module-local in-memory map, with the file's own comment stating it is not suitable for multiple instances.
The Redis fixed-window limiter with an in-process fallback that every sibling public writer uses.

existingControls: Both routes are honeypot-guarded with a fake-success response, so a bot learns nothing.
Both bound the request body before parsing and validate every field with a schema.
The access-request route does use the shared Redis limiter.
controlGaps: The sales-leads counter resets on every container restart or redeploy, and each replica enforces its own cap, so the effective limit is the stated limit multiplied by the replica count.
Neither route suppresses duplicates, so the limiter is the only bound on repeated rows.
acceptanceCriteria: The sales-leads route uses the shared Redis limiter with its own registered action, and a test asserts the module-local map is gone.
Both lead routes suppress duplicate submissions within a bounded window, with a test.
risks.residualRisk: Duplicate suppression keyed on a collapsed client address (R-26) suppresses across every visitor behind one edge point of presence, so the key must be reconsidered together with that risk.

risks.title: The only public handler that creates a user validates nothing and writes outside a transaction
preconditions: None: the route is public by design and is the current implementation.

evidence.note: The email is never validated as an email, the name has no length bound, and four further fields are unvalidated and unbounded despite their declared types.

evidence.locator: the parse and the two writes
evidence.note: A hand-written interface over a raw parse, checking only presence and a password length, then two writes that are not in one transaction.
A password policy module exists and is not used by this route.

existingControls: The role is hardcoded and the verified flag is false, so neither is client-settable — the critical control, and it is correct.
A registered rate limiter is applied first, before any parse or write.
A content-type check and a bounded body precede parsing.
If the session cannot be persisted the route fails closed with no partial, non-revocable session.
controlGaps: No schema validation, so arbitrary strings are stored as user records and the unique-email constraint is the only data-quality control.
No transaction, so a failure between the two writes leaves a candidate-role user with no candidate record — a state the response shape already anticipates.
No honeypot and no challenge, unlike both sibling lead forms.
acceptanceCriteria: Every field is validated by the repository's schema validator with explicit bounds, and the shared password policy is applied.
The user and candidate writes happen in one transaction, and a test asserts that a failure in the second leaves no user row.
An audit event records user creation.
risks.residualRisk: Validation does not prevent bulk registration of syntactically valid accounts; that bound remains the rate limiter, and the enumeration oracle is tracked separately as R-07.

risks.title: Unrelated public features share one rate-limit bucket, so each can exhaust the other's allowance
preconditions: None: the three media handlers declare the Copilot demo's action names as their own.

evidence.note: Browsing the public video hub consumes the Copilot demo's budget for that address and vice versa, so neither limit can be tuned independently.
Declares the Copilot demo's read bucket as its own.
34 registered actions; the registry enforces that an action exists but not that it is semantically distinct, and that second gap is where this sits.

existingControls: Every action string used by all 48 public route files is registered, so no public handler is silently unlimited.
The limiter fails closed on an undeclared action and writes an audit event, so inventing an action name would block the route rather than remove the limit.
controlGaps: Bucket collision between unrelated features is invisible to the registry test, which only asserts existence.
acceptanceCriteria: Dedicated actions are registered for the public media read and the view beacon, and the three handlers point at them.
A test asserts that no two unrelated route modules declare the same action name.
The stale comments that misstate the limiter's failure mode are removed as part of R-27.
risks.residualRisk: Separating buckets does not change that every visitor behind one edge point of presence still shares a bucket (R-26), which is the larger aggregation problem.

risks.title: The avatar upload accepts unsniffed bytes, bounds after buffering, and publishes to an unauthenticated static surface
preconditions: An authenticated identity of any role, because the gate is the authentication helper alone.

evidence.note: The proxy permits fifty megabytes, so the application is the only bound.
The uploads volume is mounted inside the public directory, so its contents are served as static assets with no authorization check and no policy header.

evidence.locator: the gate, the buffer and the size check
evidence.note: The buffer is materialised before the two-megabyte ceiling is applied, and no magic-byte sniffing is performed.
The sibling route sniffs magic bytes and checks the declared size before buffering; the module names that as the one deliberate hardening the avatar route lacks.

existingControls: Filenames are 128-bit random with an extension from a three-item allowlist, and the uploader's filename is never used, so the stored path is unguessable.
Only two writers exist under the public directory and both store images intended for public publication; no writer exists for tenant-scoped, site-scoped or industrial data.
The sibling cover route demonstrates the correct pattern inside the same codebase.
controlGaps: Content type is taken on trust, so a file whose bytes are not the declared image type is stored and served from the application's own origin.
The ceiling is applied after the whole body is in memory, so the proxy's fifty-megabyte allowance is the practical limit per request.
Static serving bypasses middleware entirely, so neither authorization nor the content-security policy applies to the served object.
acceptanceCriteria: The avatar route sniffs magic bytes using the same helper as the cover route, with a test that a mislabelled file is refused.
The declared size is checked before buffering and the real length re-checked after, with a test at the boundary.
A response header policy for the static uploads path is recorded, or the objects are moved out of the public directory and served through an authorizing route.
risks.residualRisk: Magic-byte sniffing identifies a container, not its contents; an image that is a valid image and also carries a payload for some other consumer is still accepted. Serving user-supplied bytes from the application's own origin remains an architectural choice tracked by the header policy criterion.

risks.title: Two public-content behaviours need a policy decision rather than a fix
preconditions: None: both behaviours are the current, deliberate implementation.

evidence.note: A HEAD request returns a one-year locale cookie; this is the internationalisation library's documented negotiation behaviour and carries no identity.
The authentication helper alone, with no role and no permission.

existingControls: An authenticated identity is required to upload, so the surface is not anonymous.
The locale cookie carries no identity and is set by a library behaviour rather than an application decision.
controlGaps: No requirement exists stating who may publish an avatar to the public static surface, so there is nothing to enforce.
No decision exists on whether a nominally side-effect-free method may set state, nor on the cookie's consent classification.
acceptanceCriteria: The owner records which roles may publish an avatar; the route then enforces it and a test asserts the refusal for a role below the requirement.
The owner records whether a HEAD request may set the locale cookie and under which consent classification; the answer is then expressed in the cookie policy document or in code.
risks.residualRisk: Until the upload requirement is recorded, the hardening in R-22 improves the handling of the bytes without settling who may submit them.

risks.title: The origin is directly reachable from the internet, so the edge can be bypassed
preconditions: None. A request from a vantage independent of both the production host and the audit environment reached the origin and was answered with the origin's own signature.

evidence.note: No request-rate or connection limits and no trusted-proxy configuration, so the proxy adds no protection of its own.
The direct origin response carried the proxy's own server signature with no edge headers, which is mutually exclusive with the edge signature and identical to the host's own self-check.
No host-level restriction of any kind: both address families bound on all interfaces, the host firewall allows anywhere, and the container chain carries no allowlist.

existingControls: Every application gate still applies to a direct request: authentication, authorization and the per-action rate limiter are in the application, not at the edge.
Transport security is terminated at the origin with a valid certificate, so a direct request is still encrypted.
Reaching the origin directly makes the trusted client-address header carry the real caller, so the rate limiter becomes more accurate, not less.
controlGaps: Edge denial-of-service absorption, caching and any edge-layer filtering are all bypassable.
The proxy has no request-rate or connection limit of its own to compensate.
Whether a provider-level filter exists is unknown; what is measured is that no restriction was enforced for the observed vantage.
acceptanceCriteria: Inbound traffic on the public ports is accepted only from the edge provider's published ranges, enforced in the container chain rather than in the host firewall alone, with a documented automated procedure for refreshing those ranges.
Request-rate and connection limits exist at the proxy as defence in depth.
The closure is re-verified from an independent external vantage, and the observation is recorded with the same rigour as the opening evidence.
risks.residualRisk: An allowlist of a provider's published ranges is only as current as its refresh procedure, and it does not protect against an attacker who proxies through the edge itself. The unexplained path instability in R-30 means a single successful verification does not prove a stable posture.

risks.title: Strict transport security is set nowhere, at any layer
preconditions: An active network position between the visitor and the platform for a downgrade or interception attempt.

evidence.note: Zero header directives, so the transport-security header is not set at the proxy.
The header was confirmed absent on the edge-served response, on the host's own self-check and on the direct origin response from an independent external vantage.
Sets four security headers and states that transport security is set exclusively by the proxy — a control documented in one place and implemented in none.

existingControls: Port eighty answers with a permanent redirect to the secure scheme.
Authentication cookies are marked secure in production, so a downgraded request does not carry them.
Four other response security headers are present and verified.
controlGaps: No instruction to the browser to refuse an insecure connection, so the first request of a session has no protection and no preload entry exists.
The absence is confirmed from three vantages, so neither the edge nor the origin supplies it.
acceptanceCriteria: The transport-security header is emitted with a defensible duration and subdomain policy, at the layer the configuration says owns it, and the documentation and the implementation agree.
The header is verified present on a response from the edge and on a direct origin response.
A decision on preload registration is recorded, because it is difficult to reverse.
risks.residualRisk: The header protects only browsers that have already seen it, so the very first contact remains unprotected until a preload entry exists; preloading is close to irreversible and is therefore a deliberate decision rather than a default.

risks.title: The application's idea of the client address is an edge point of presence, and two extractors disagree
preconditions: None: the edge is in front of the origin in production and the trusted header is set from the proxy's peer.

evidence.note: The trusted header is set from the proxy's own peer address, and no trusted-proxy directive exists to recover the original caller.
The edge supplies the real caller on every request; it is neither stripped nor rewritten, and is read by no code.

evidence.locator: the client-address resolver and its comment
evidence.note: The comment asserts the deployment has no edge provider in front, which production contradicts, and the mitigation the comment itself prescribes was never applied.

existingControls: Spoofing is genuinely prevented: the proxy overwrites the trusted header, and every client-settable alternative is ignored. This is a deliberate and correct choice that a prior phase made after a real defect.
The authentication limiter is fail-closed and action-isolated, so over-aggregation tightens rather than loosens it.
controlGaps: Every visitor behind one edge point of presence shares a single rate-limit bucket, so one noisy visitor can exhaust the budget for many.
The stored address pseudonyms identify an edge node rather than a visitor, so attribution is lost and the privacy control in R-16 protects a value that was never personal.
Two independent extractors with no shared code mean a fix to one does not reach the other, and neither normalises address forms.
acceptanceCriteria: The proxy declares the edge provider's ranges as trusted and recovers the original caller into the header the application already trusts, with the hop count matched to the real topology rather than copied from an example.
Client-supplied forwarding and edge headers are cleared at the trust boundary rather than relying on later overwrite ordering.
One server-side resolver is used by both current extractors and returns a typed result rather than a sentinel string, with deterministic normalisation of address forms.
The comment that asserts the wrong topology is corrected as part of R-27.
risks.residualRisk: Trusting the edge's header is only safe while the origin cannot be reached directly; this remediation therefore depends on R-24 being closed first, or a direct request could present a forged caller address. That ordering is the single most important sequencing constraint in this register.

risks.title: Production comments assert a safety property the code does not have, and one already corrupted a security document
preconditions: None: the comments are in the current source.

evidence.note: The corrected section: the first version of that document took the claim from the comment instead of from the limiter and published the inverted statement.
Asserts the limiter fails open on an unknown action.
The limiter refuses, returns a refusal, logs at error level and writes an audit event — the opposite of the comment.

existingControls: The limiter's real behaviour is comprehensively fail-closed and is covered by a registry test.
The error was caught and corrected inside this programme, with the correction left visible in the document.
controlGaps: A comment that misstates a safety property in the dangerous direction will be believed by the next reader, and already was.
Nothing ties a comment about a control to the control's actual behaviour.
acceptanceCriteria: The two comments are corrected to state the limiter's real failure mode, and the client-address comment that asserts the wrong topology is corrected with them.
Where a comment states a safety property, it names the test that proves it.
risks.residualRisk: Correcting three comments does not create a mechanism that keeps comments and behaviour aligned; the naming convention in the second criterion is a convention, not a gate.

risks.title: The platform discloses its framework and does not suppress server version tokens
preconditions: None: both are observable on a single unauthenticated request.

evidence.note: The directive that suppresses the proxy's version token is absent.
The framework header is present on every response; it is a hardening opportunity, not a critical vulnerability.
The framework header can be suppressed by one configuration flag.

existingControls: Four other response security headers are present, and the content-security policy is nonce-based per request.
controlGaps: Both values narrow an attacker's guesswork about the stack for no functional benefit.
acceptanceCriteria: The framework header is disabled in configuration and the proxy's version token is suppressed.
Both absences are verified on a response from the edge and on a direct origin response.
risks.residualRisk: Version suppression is cosmetic against a determined attacker, who can fingerprint the stack from behaviour; it removes a free hint, nothing more.

risks.title: Security-relevant configuration and documentation have drifted from the code they describe
preconditions: None: each item is a current inconsistency between a statement and the code or data it describes.

evidence.note: Lists an address that is on no interface of the production host — harmless as a matching token, and the direct cause of one invalid audit test.

One document calls the signing-variable precondition unverified while the other records the owner-supplied presence check and the verdict that the flaw is not active in the observed container. The second is the later and correct record; the first was never updated, and this register was built from the stale sentence until the reconciliation.
States 79 selftests in one section and 75 in two others, because the corrective revision updated only the first.
States route-file, handler and public-writer counts that the committed inventory on this source state contradicts.
Registers a guard that has zero definitions and zero uses anywhere in the codebase, so the token can never match.

existingControls: The route inventory is kept from drifting against the source tree by a committed check that passes on this source state.
Each drift listed here was found by reading the artifacts against the code rather than by trusting either.
controlGaps: A guard name that does not exist invites a future change to invent one, or to assume a boundary is enforced where it is not.
A narrative document and a generated artifact describing the same surface have no mechanism keeping them consistent.
A document that quotes its own tool's test count has no gate asserting the quote.
Two documents in the same phase recorded opposite statuses for one precondition, and nothing detected it; the register now carries a gate that would, but the source documents still disagree.
acceptanceCriteria: The stale server name is removed from the proxy configuration, and the phantom guard token is removed from the classifier.
The attack-surface narrative is regenerated from, or checked against, the committed inventory, so the two cannot disagree silently.
The classification document's quoted test count is corrected, and a gate asserts that any count a security document quotes from its own tool matches the tool's output.
The legacy-token document's precondition sentence is corrected to match the recorded evidence, so the two S0 documents no longer disagree.
risks.residualRisk: NEITHER SOURCE-DOCUMENT DEFECT IS FIXED BY THIS PHASE. The order authorising S1 limits the deliverables to four paths and neither of those documents is among them, so both are disclosed here rather than corrected: the quoted test count, which is cosmetic because no count bearing on a security conclusion is affected, and the precondition sentence, which is not cosmetic because this register was built from it and reported a settled condition as unknown until the reconciliation. Both remain open against the committed S0 documents.

risks.title: The network path to the origin address was unstable between two observations and the mechanism is unknown
preconditions: None for the gap: two genuine observations of the same destination disagreed within half a minute.

evidence.note: Recorded with every candidate mechanism explicitly unevidenced: no evidence for provider address import, transit, proxying, carrier interception, anycast or resolution variance.
The same device, command and destination received an edge-fronted response and then a direct origin response twenty-three seconds apart, with no proxy configured on either run.

existingControls: Both observations are recorded rather than reconciled by discarding one, so the instability is visible instead of averaged away.
The reachability conclusion does not depend on explaining the instability, because it rests on the direct response's own signature.
controlGaps: Any future verification of R-24's closure from one request could be misled by the same instability, in either direction.
No monitoring exists that would detect the path changing.
acceptanceCriteria: Any verification of the origin posture uses repeated observations over time from more than one vantage, not a single request.
A recorded explanation of the instability exists, or the inability to explain it is accepted in writing with the monitoring that compensates.
risks.residualRisk: Explaining the instability may require evidence from the network provider that this programme cannot obtain, in which case the compensating control is repeated observation rather than understanding.

risks.title: The health surface is unauthenticated and its access logging is disabled at the proxy
preconditions: None: the proxy forwards the health path on the insecure port with access logging switched off.

evidence.note: Proxied on the insecure port with access logging disabled, while every other path on that port is redirected.
Classified as an internal health surface by the committed inventory.

existingControls: The two handlers are declared as an internal health surface in the inventory rather than being silently unclassified.
The readiness probe is the one place in the platform that records an infrastructure failure properly.
controlGaps: Requests to the health surface leave no proxy access record, so probing it is invisible at that layer.
The surface is reachable without authentication on the insecure port, so it is also reachable directly at the origin.
acceptanceCriteria: The health response is confirmed to disclose no version, dependency state or internal address, with a test on the response shape.
A decision is recorded on whether access logging must stay off, and if it stays off the reason is written down.
risks.residualRisk: A health endpoint has to be reachable by whatever checks it; the remediation bounds what it reveals rather than who can reach it.

risks.title: A silent fallback accepts writes into process memory and reports success, including the store it claims to have used
preconditions: The database client is null, or any Prisma call throws — a timeout, pool exhaustion or constraint error is enough, not only a full outage.
No runtime observation exists: this is what the code will do, traced to the statement that does it.

evidence.note: 69 fallback points, 34 inside bare catch blocks, writes included, zero logging; 67 of them outage-conditional, reproduced from consumer edges and equal to the manual count per file.
Answers with a field asserting the storage mode after the write fell back to process memory, and the same shape exists on the knowledge and analysis routes.
The one independent path, which returns the session store both when the mode is not database and when the client is null.
A session repository is constructed up front and returned to on every operation, both on a null client and from a bare catch.

existingControls: Tenant isolation is preserved: the session repositories apply the same owner predicate, and a null owner is an impossible sentinel that sees nothing.
Role enforcement is upstream in the route layer and is unaffected.
The public graph reads published content only, so the fallback is not a disclosure on that surface.
The enterprise-resource surface demonstrates the correct alternative in the same codebase: a controlled refusal with a stable code and no degradation to process storage.
controlGaps: A mutation is accepted, reported as successful, survives only until the container restarts, is invisible to any other replica, and gets a non-conforming identifier.
Nothing is logged inside those catch blocks, so neither the caller nor the operator learns that the write did not land.
No audit row records the mutation, because the audit writer is itself database-backed.
The response states which store was used, and that statement is false.
acceptanceCriteria: In database mode no sensitive read or write falls back to process memory: each of the 67 outage-conditional paths answers the controlled refusal the enterprise-resource layer already models, with a stable error code.
No response asserts a storage mode that was not used; either the request is refused, or the mode actually used is stated.
The deterministic call-site gate runs in continuous integration so a new unguarded fallback fails the build.
A test asserts that a write attempted while the client is unavailable leaves no caller-visible success.
risks.residualRisk: Refusing converts a silent integrity defect into a visible outage, which is correct but changes the platform's availability profile; the two unconditional delegations that never had a database implementation are a separate design decision and are not closed by this criterion.

risks.title: An outage is acknowledged to an external party that will therefore never retry
preconditions: The database client is unavailable at the moment an industrial gateway posts telemetry or a payment provider delivers an event.

evidence.note: Both are traced to their terminal response, with retry behaviour recorded as absent and the audit row recorded as attempted and failing.
Returns early on a null client while the route answers success with an ignored outcome, so the provider treats the event as delivered.
The rejection record is itself database-backed and fails on the same outage.
Returns early on a null client while the route answers created with a zero count, so the gateway treats the readings as stored.

existingControls: Replay protection on the gateway envelope is unaffected: the timestamp, nonce and idempotency key are inside the signed field set.
The gateway surface does not accept a tenant identifier from the envelope, so no cross-tenant claim is possible.
controlGaps: A success status is the instruction not to resend, so the data is lost rather than delayed — the one failure mode a buffering edge device cannot recover from.
The audit row that would record the loss is attempted on the same unavailable client.
A provider that has been told an event was received will not redeliver it, so billing state diverges silently.
acceptanceCriteria: Telemetry ingestion answers a server-error status when the readings were not stored, writes no ingestion audit row, and lets the gateway buffer and retry; a test asserts the status and the absence of the audit row.

A webhook the platform could not durably claim answers a server-error status so the provider retries, and no event is marked processed, ignored or failed on a path that returned early without a client.
A fault-injection rehearsal with the database made unavailable shows no acknowledgement emitted for an unpersisted event, and a test asserts the same.
risks.residualRisk: Returning an error invites provider retry storms during a long outage, so the remediation needs a bounded retry contract on both surfaces; the gateway's offline buffering capacity is asserted by design documents outside this repository and cannot be verified here.

risks.title: Gateway revocation and heartbeat report security outcomes that did not happen
preconditions: The database client is unavailable at the moment an operator revokes a gateway, or when a gateway heartbeats.

evidence.note: Recorded as the most consequential mis-statement found in that revision: an operator revoking a credential they believe is compromised is told the job is already done, nothing happened, and no audit row records the attempt.
Writes a heartbeat audit event and meters the call without checking that anything was persisted.
Answers not found or already revoked, with the revocation audit event written only after the guard.
Both return early on a null client; the revoke helper returns nothing to distinguish an outage from a missing record.

existingControls: The gateway credential itself is a proof-of-possession signature rather than a shared reference string, so revocation is the only way to invalidate it and there is no weaker path.
Enrollment, rotation and revocation routes all exist, so the operator has the right surface to act through.
controlGaps: A revocation that silently did nothing is reported as a revocation that was already done, which is the one answer that stops an operator from responding further.
No audit row records the attempt, so the incident timeline loses the operator's action as well as its failure.
An audit row asserting a heartbeat that was never recorded makes the audit trail actively wrong rather than merely incomplete.
acceptanceCriteria: Revocation distinguishes an unavailable database from a missing record and never reports already revoked for an outage; a test asserts the refusal status for each condition separately.
The attempt is audited before the outcome is known, so a failed revocation leaves a trace.
The heartbeat route checks that the write happened before auditing or metering it, proven by a test and by a fault-injection rehearsal with the database made unavailable.
risks.residualRisk: Auditing the attempt requires an audit path that survives a database outage, which R-38's remediation must supply; until then the attempt trace is as fragile as the operation it records.

risks.title: Industrial and twin reads present an outage as an empty success, so an operator reads zero rather than unknown
preconditions: The database client is unavailable while an operator views an industrial, twin, predictive, time-series or multi-site surface.

evidence.note: Two numbers kept deliberately apart: 26 on the historic single-line shape and 98 on the semantic definition, with the 72 additional sites distributed across 33 files.
Return an empty collection with a success status when the client is null.
The contrast that makes the defect precise: here an empty collection is correct and fail-closed, because it means the caller may see nothing.

existingControls: Confidentiality is fail-closed in the only sense that matters here: no database means no rows, so nothing is disclosed.
Tenant isolation is unaffected.
controlGaps: An empty collection means both you may see nothing and I could not ask, and the client cannot tell them apart.
On a plant surface that renders as zero alarms, zero assets and zero telemetry during an outage, which is a safety-relevant misrepresentation.
Health functions report zeros rather than unknown, so the surface that should expose the outage also hides it.
acceptanceCriteria: A third state exists and is distinguishable by the client: an empty collection means nothing, and an unavailable data source is its own signal.
The 26 legacy sites are converted first and the remaining semantic sites thereafter, with the counts tracked against the committed inventory.
Health functions report unknown rather than zero when they could not ask, with a test.
A plant-facing surface renders the unavailable state visibly rather than as zero, verified on at least one industrial view during a fault-injection rehearsal.
risks.residualRisk: A third state has to be handled by every client of these functions, so the change is wider than the server-side sites; the authorization-scope functions that legitimately return an empty collection must not be swept into it.

risks.title: An outage is rendered as a wrong domain answer: not found, duplicate, conflict, or an authentication failure
preconditions: The database client is unavailable while a user performs an update, a compliance write, an academy read or a public certificate verification.

evidence.note: The create and update pairs diverge: creates answer a service-unavailable status while updates answer not found, and two creators answer a duplicate-key status for the same condition.
Organization, billing, knowledge and platform-key writes answer an unprocessable status while echoing an internal reason string, and compliance writes answer a conflict status.
Answers success with the holder name rendered as unknown during an outage.
Collapses four distinct conditions into one null, after which the handler answers that authentication is required.

existingControls: No confidentiality boundary is crossed by any of these responses.
The create siblings of the diverging update paths already answer the correct service-unavailable status, so the right pattern exists in the same modules.
One module in the automation subsystem already models the correct write-error mapping and is the pattern to copy.
controlGaps: On a plant surface, not found is a statement about the equipment rather than about the platform.
An outage reported as an authentication failure sends users to re-authenticate pointlessly and fills every authentication-failure monitor with infrastructure noise.
An internal reason string echoed to a caller is an information-disclosure defect on top of the wrong status.
One academy module answers the same condition two incompatible ways across six routes.
acceptanceCriteria: A database outage answers a service-unavailable status everywhere, never a not-found, duplicate, conflict, unprocessable or authentication status, and no internal reason string is echoed.
The industrial and twin update paths match their create siblings, with a test per pair.
The academy resolver separates its four conditions and the six routes agree with each other, with a test per route.
An authentication-failure monitor is shown not to fire for a simulated outage.
risks.residualRisk: Changing a status code is a client-visible contract change on roughly twenty surfaces, so it needs coordinated client handling; the public certificate route's unknown-holder response is a product decision about whether to answer at all during an outage.

risks.title: Metering and audit evidence is lost on every degraded path, and the audit writer shares the failure
preconditions: The database client is unavailable while any audited mutation or metered call occurs.

evidence.note: The audit-loss outcome class holds 146 unique identifiers: writes and deletes for which no row records what happened.
Usage records are dropped silently when the client is unavailable.
The audit writer is itself database-backed, so a mutation accepted into process memory leaves no audit row.

existingControls: Correlation identifiers exist on the audit model and in the logger, so a surviving trace can be joined when one exists.
The metering outbox worker has a delivery path at the web tier, so metering is not purely fire-and-forget by design.
controlGaps: The audit trail and the operation it records share one failure domain, so the evidence disappears exactly when it is most needed.
Usage records that are dropped cannot be reconstructed, so billing under-counts silently.
acceptanceCriteria: An audit path exists that does not share the primary database's failure domain, at least for security-relevant events: authentication, authorization refusal, revocation, erasure and export.
Metering either refuses the call or records the usage durably; silent loss is removed, with a test.
A rehearsal demonstrates that a security-relevant event during a database outage still produces evidence.
risks.residualRisk: A second audit sink adds a component that itself can fail and must be protected to the same standard as the primary; choosing one is an architectural decision this register does not make.

risks.title: The audit trail has no tamper evidence and its tenancy columns are nullable
preconditions: Database write access, which the application itself holds, because the migration role and the runtime role are the same identity.

evidence.note: A tamper-evident audit trail does not currently exist, and the separate immutable reasoning-run ledger does not make this table tamper-evident.
No previous-hash, chain, signature or append-only enforcement field, and the organization, outcome and correlation columns are all nullable.
Around twenty namespaced catalogues write into that plain append table.

existingControls: The table is indexed on action, user, organization, creation time and correlation, so it is usable as a trail.
A separate immutable ledger exists for reasoning runs, which demonstrates the pattern is understood in this codebase.
controlGaps: A row can be altered or deleted with no detectable trace, so the trail cannot evidence anything against someone who holds database access.
Nullable tenancy means a row can exist without identifying the organization it belongs to, which weakens both tenant attribution and retention.
acceptanceCriteria: Security-relevant audit rows carry a verifiable chain or signature, with a verifier that detects an altered or removed row and a test that proves the detection.
The organization column is required for every row that belongs to an organization, enforced at write time.
A retention and protection posture is recorded for the trail, including who can delete and under what approval.
risks.residualRisk: A chain detects tampering; it does not prevent it, and it is only as trustworthy as the place its anchor is kept. Separating the runtime role from the migration role (R-47) is what would stop the application's own credential from rewriting history.

risks.title: Brute-force detection is silently disabled while the database is unavailable
preconditions: The database client is unavailable during a login attempt.

evidence.note: The account-lock check's fail-open is masked because token issuance throws and the handler answers a service-unavailable status, so no login can succeed during the same outage; what is lost is the detection.
No counter, no failed-login event and no lockout state are recorded when the client is unavailable.

existingControls: The outage that disables detection also prevents any login from succeeding, so this is a loss of detection rather than of enforcement.
The address-keyed rate limiter is Redis-backed with an in-process fallback and is independent of the database, so online guessing is still bounded.
controlGaps: An attacker can probe during an outage without accumulating lockout state or leaving failed-login evidence, so the attempt is invisible afterwards.
The masking depends on a second component's behaviour rather than on an explicit decision, so a future change to token issuance could unmask the fail-open.
acceptanceCriteria: The account-lock check fails closed explicitly rather than relying on token issuance to throw, with a test.
Failed-login evidence is recorded on a path that survives a database outage, demonstrated by a fault-injection rehearsal and matching R-37's audit criterion.
risks.residualRisk: Recording failures outside the database depends on R-37's second sink; until that exists, the detection gap narrows rather than closes.

risks.title: Degraded paths are invisible: almost every exception path and half the call sites are silent
preconditions: None: the silence is a property of the current source, independent of whether a failure has occurred.

evidence.note: 119 of 124 exception edges are silent; only five log.
211 of 392 call sites carry no logging on the degraded path, and the infrastructure-failure logger fires in exactly three places on a null client across the whole platform.
The one place that records the condition properly, and the shape the rest should copy.

existingControls: Structured logging, correlation identifiers and a safe error describer all exist and are used elsewhere.
The readiness probe demonstrates the correct instrumentation inside this codebase.
The deterministic inventory now measures the silence, so it can be tracked rather than guessed.
controlGaps: An outage or a transient error is invisible to an operator almost everywhere, so a silent integrity defect has no detection path at all.
Without a metric there is no way to know how often the fallback in R-32 has actually been taken.
acceptanceCriteria: Every degraded path records an infrastructure failure with a correlation identifier, a subsystem and a failure class, and no secret, plus a metric.
An alert exists for a non-zero rate of degraded-path events in production.
The deterministic inventory's silence counters run as a gate in continuous integration and are tracked over time, so the number must fall rather than drift.
risks.residualRisk: Instrumenting 211 sites is a wide, low-risk change that will generate noise before it generates signal; the alert threshold is a judgement that needs a baseline the platform does not yet have.

risks.title: A partial failure between two writes can leave a suspended member's sessions live
preconditions: The suspension write must commit and the session generation bump must then fail — a partial database failure between two statements.
The null-client path is unreachable: the member-status write has already refused on the identical condition.

evidence.note: Organization surfaces stay denied by the per-request role re-read; non-organization sessions survive until expiry.
Its result is discarded by the caller, so a failure to bump the generation is not detected.
The status write refuses on a null client before the revocation call is reached, which is why only the exception path matters.

existingControls: Organization surfaces re-read the member's role per request, so the suspended member is still refused there.
The session store is fail-closed on every other condition, including an unreachable database.
The null-client path is masked by an earlier refusal, so only a mid-operation exception reaches this state.
controlGaps: The two writes are not atomic and the second one's result is not checked, so the suspension is partially applied with no signal.
Sessions outside the organization surfaces remain valid until expiry.
acceptanceCriteria: The status update and the session-generation bump happen in one transaction, or the revocation result is checked and the operation fails as a whole.
A test asserts that a failure in the second write leaves the member unsuspended rather than half-suspended.
risks.residualRisk: An atomic suspension still leaves already-issued tokens valid until the next revocation check, which is the general property of the session model rather than a defect of this path.

risks.title: Dead product surface refuses correctly where nothing can observe it, including all site-membership management
preconditions: None: the absence of callers is a property of the current source.

evidence.note: Twenty-seven consumer edges and nine exported functions with no caller; each refuses correctly, and each is surface whose refusal nothing can observe.
No caller, corroborating the privileged-route finding that ownership transfer is declared but unimplemented.
The whole module has no caller in the application or the scripts, so site membership can neither be read nor managed through the product.

existingControls: Every one of these functions refuses correctly when it is called, so the dead surface is not a weak surface.
The deterministic inventory enumerates them mechanically rather than from memory, so the list is reviewable.
controlGaps: Site membership is a security control with no administrative surface, so the thinness in R-10 cannot even be managed.
A schema column with no writer is either missing functionality or stale schema, and either way nothing tests it.
