Dead code inflates the apparent control surface, which is how a reviewer concludes a boundary is managed when it is not.
acceptanceCriteria: Each of the nine exported functions and the unwritten column is either wired to a product surface or deleted, with the decision recorded.
Site membership management is addressed first, because it is a security control rather than a convenience.
A gate reports an exported function in a security-relevant module with no caller, so the class cannot silently reappear.
risks.residualRisk: Deleting a function that an unreleased feature intends to use is a product decision, not a security one; the gate reports rather than decides, and a reported function may legitimately be kept.

risks.title: Continuous integration carries no security scanning of any kind
preconditions: None: the absence is a property of the 13 committed workflows.

evidence.note: Eleven named security tool families return zero occurrences across every workflow.
The only dependency control, governed by a committed exceptions file.
Walks generated manifests so they cannot carry a secret value and allows key names explicitly; it never examines the source tree or history.

existingControls: Third-party actions are pinned by commit, the integration workflow runs with read-only content permissions, and deployment is manual with a protected environment.
The dependency-audit gate is real, governed by an explicit exceptions file with expiry dates.
A restore rehearsal job exists.
controlGaps: No static analysis, so an introduced injection or authorization defect has no automated detector.
No secret scanning of the tree or of history anywhere, so a committed credential would be found only by a human.
No container or infrastructure scanning, no dynamic testing, no software bill of materials and no artifact signing, so a built image has no provenance.
acceptanceCriteria: Static analysis, secret scanning of the tree and of history, container image scanning and infrastructure scanning all run on every pull request, with a documented triage path for findings.
A software bill of materials is produced per build and the image is signed, so a deployed artifact can be traced to a commit.
Each new gate starts as reporting-only with a recorded date on which it becomes blocking, so the programme is not stopped by a backlog on day one.
risks.residualRisk: Scanners produce findings the team must triage; without the governance file the dependency gate already has, a new scanner becomes an ignored red light, which is worse than its absence because it teaches the team to ignore gates.

risks.title: Five dependency advisories are open in the production tree
preconditions: Each advisory has its own exploitation precondition, which the register entries do not restate and this phase did not assess.

evidence.note: The process by which an advisory is accepted, with an expiry, rather than silently ignored.
All five are medium, all five state that an in-range update clears the advisory, and none is marked a release blocker.
The control that keeps the set from growing unnoticed.

existingControls: A committed gate measures the advisory set on every pull request, and a governance file records accepted exceptions with expiry dates.
The deliberate decision not to change the lockfile inside a security-review change is recorded in each entry, so the deferral is explicit rather than accidental.
controlGaps: Five advisories remain open in the production tree, each clearable by an in-range update that has not been applied.
No exploitability assessment exists for any of the five in the context of how this platform uses the package.
acceptanceCriteria: Each of the five is updated in range, or accepted through the governance file with a reason and an expiry, with the dependency-audit gate green either way.
For any acceptance, the reachability of the vulnerable code path in this platform is stated rather than assumed.
risks.residualRisk: An advisory count is not a risk measure: a reachable medium matters more than an unreachable high, and nothing in this register establishes reachability for these five.

risks.title: Twenty-nine Phase 99 remediations are inherited as fixed rather than re-verified in this programme
preconditions: None: the gap is that this programme did not re-execute the evidence behind those closures.

evidence.note: Phase 99 already built a security programme for this repository, and its findings are reconciled with each finding's status re-verified rather than inherited, because this repository has a recorded history of findings going stale in both directions.
Twenty-nine entries carry a verified-fixed status, each with a retest reference.
The test matrix behind those closures, which this programme did not execute.

existingControls: Each closure carries a retest reference, so the evidence is named and reachable.

Several of the fixes were independently corroborated in this programme as a side effect: the published-predicate fix, the client-address keying fix, the certificate-expiry fix and the four site allow-list fixes were all observed in the current source while other work was done.
The five tool defects in this set were found, fixed and pinned by selftests inside this programme, so their closure is this programme's own evidence rather than inherited.
controlGaps: No test behind those closures was executed in this worktree, because it has no installed dependencies, so twenty-four of the twenty-nine rest on a prior phase's word.
A fix verified once is not a fix that stays verified; nothing in this programme re-measured them.
acceptanceCriteria: The Phase 99 test matrix is executed in an environment where it can run, and the result is reported per finding rather than in aggregate.
Any finding whose retest no longer passes is reopened in this register with its own risk entry.
The regression tests for the critical and high closures run in continuous integration, so a reintroduction fails the build.
risks.residualRisk: Re-verification needs a working dependency installation, which this programme's worktree deliberately does not have; until it is run elsewhere, the critical session-cookie finding and the three high findings about session tokens, mass assignment and site allow-lists are closed on inherited evidence.

risks.title: Containers run without runtime hardening, images are unpinned, and the development compose publishes data ports
preconditions: For the hardening gaps: an attacker must first achieve execution inside a container, which nothing in this register demonstrates.
For the development compose: that file would have to be used on a reachable host. The owner has confirmed production uses the production file.

evidence.note: None of the read-only root, capability-dropping, privilege-escalation, temporary-filesystem or resource-limit controls is present, the internal network is a plain bridge so containers keep outbound egress, and all four images are tags rather than digests.
Publishes both data-service ports, uses a weak default database password and sets no cache password at all.
What is hardened and what is absent, side by side: every stage runs non-root, no data port is published in production and the container runtime socket is not mounted.

existingControls: Every image stage runs as a non-root user, which is the single most valuable container control and it is present.
Neither data service publishes a host port in production, the container runtime socket is not mounted, health checks and log rotation exist, and nothing applies migrations on boot.
Worker images carry one dependency-free script each with no database credential.
controlGaps: A compromised process can write anywhere in its filesystem, keep every capability, escalate privileges and consume unbounded memory.
Outbound egress from every container is unrestricted, which is what turns an execution foothold into exfiltration.
Unpinned images mean the bytes that run are not the bytes that were reviewed, which is the supply-chain half of R-43.
A weak default password is a fallback that works, so it can reach production through an unset variable.
acceptanceCriteria: Production services drop capabilities, forbid privilege escalation, run with a read-only root filesystem plus explicit writable mounts, and carry memory and process limits.
The internal network is genuinely internal, with egress permitted only where a service needs it and documented per service.
Every image is pinned by digest, with a documented refresh procedure.
No weak default credential remains reachable: an unset password fails the start rather than falling back.
Rollback steps are documented for each change and exercised in a rehearsal before the change ships, because these are the changes most likely to stop a healthy service.
risks.residualRisk: A read-only root filesystem and capability dropping break services that write outside their declared mounts, so this must be rehearsed before it is applied; the development compose is a deliberate convenience and the remediation is to make it unusable on a reachable host rather than to harden it.

risks.title: The database connection is unencrypted by configuration and one identity holds both migration and runtime rights
preconditions: For interception: a position on the container network, which is not reachable from outside the host.
For the role concentration: any defect that lets a request influence a query reaches an identity that can also change the schema.

evidence.note: Connection encryption is not configured in the repository and the migration role and the runtime role are not separated in anything found in S0.
One connection string from the environment; whoever holds the credential holds both sets of rights.
One adapter built from one connection string, cached for the process.

existingControls: Traffic stays on an internal container network with no published port, so interception requires a foothold on the host.
Migrations are applied by a dedicated non-root stage as an explicit step, never on boot, so the schema is not changed by the running service in normal operation.
controlGaps: Transport encryption is absent by configuration rather than by decision, so it is not stated anywhere that the internal network is the control.
The application's own credential can alter the schema and rewrite the audit trail, which is what makes R-38's tamper evidence unenforceable against the application itself.
Row-level security cannot be meaningfully applied while one identity holds both rights, which is why R-09 depends on this.
acceptanceCriteria: A runtime role exists that cannot alter the schema and cannot delete from the audit trail, and the application uses it.
The migration role is used only by the migration step, with its credential unavailable to the running service.
Transport encryption is either enabled and recorded, or its absence is accepted in writing with the internal network named as the compensating control.
A rehearsal proves the application still works under the restricted role before the change ships.
risks.residualRisk: Role separation is a migration of its own and will surface every place the application quietly relied on schema rights; it is a prerequisite for both R-09 and R-38, which is why it is scheduled with them rather than after them.

risks.title: Traffic inside the cluster is unencrypted between the proxy, the application and the cache
preconditions: A position on the container network, which requires a foothold on the host or inside a container.

evidence.note: Every request crosses from the proxy to the application as plain traffic on a bridge network, with no identity between the two.
The cache has no transport encryption configured and is in-network only.
Connects with a URL and a password and no transport-security options.

existingControls: Neither hop is reachable from outside the host: no port is published for the application or the cache.
The cache requires a password in production.
Session cookies cross this hop already encrypted at the application layer in the sense that they are opaque signed tokens, so the hop does not expose a password.
controlGaps: Anything on the container network can read every request and every cached value, including rate-limit state and session-adjacent data.
There is no identity between the proxy and the application, so any container can impersonate the proxy.
acceptanceCriteria: A decision is recorded on whether intra-cluster encryption is adopted, with the internal network named as the alternative control if it is not.
If it is not adopted, the internal network is made genuinely internal as part of R-46, so the compensating control actually holds.
risks.residualRisk: Encrypting internal hops adds certificate lifecycle management to a platform that does not yet have one for its gateway boundary either; accepting the internal network as the control is defensible only once that network is genuinely closed.

risks.title: The gateway boundary is per-gateway shared-secret authentication, not the mutual certificate design the target architecture requires
preconditions: To impersonate a gateway an attacker needs that gateway's signing secret, which is resolved from the environment and stored in no database model.
Whether one gateway's secret works against another gateway's identifier depends on key separation in the secret provider, which was not verified.

evidence.note: The honest statement of the gap: what exists is per-gateway authentication with environment-resolved secrets plus application-layer replay fields, which is a real control and a real improvement over the prior design, and is not mutual certificate authentication.

No mutual transport authentication, no per-device certificate, no certificate lifecycle, no expiry monitoring and no dual-key validation window; rotation and revocation routes exist but the certificate machinery does not.

evidence.locator: the algorithm list and the rejection
evidence.note: One message-authentication algorithm is accepted and anything else is rejected; there is no certificate path.

existingControls: Authentication is proof of possession rather than knowledge of a reference string, which a prior phase fixed deliberately.
The tenant is one of the signed fields and is read from the gateway's own record, so a forged envelope cannot claim another organization.
Replay is bounded by a timestamp, a nonce and an idempotency key, all inside the signed field set, with a timing-safe comparison.
No model stores key material and no secret or signature is logged or returned.
Enrollment, rotation and revocation routes all exist.
controlGaps: A shared secret cannot be attested to a device, so a copied secret is indistinguishable from the device.

No certificate lifecycle means no expiry, no renewal and no dual-key window, so rotation is an operational event rather than a routine one — and R-34 shows revocation can currently report success without acting.
Cross-gateway key separation is unverified, so the blast radius of one compromised secret is unknown.
acceptanceCriteria: Cross-gateway key separation is established by reading the secret provider's key derivation, and a test proves one gateway's secret fails against another's identifier.
A key lifecycle exists: expiry, a dual-key validation window for rotation, and monitoring that reports a key approaching expiry.
A decision is recorded on mutual certificate authentication with a target phase, or its absence is formally accepted with the compensating controls named.
Revocation is proven effective end to end, which requires R-34 to be closed first.
risks.residualRisk: Gateway properties asserted by design documents outside this repository — outbound-only initiation, offline buffering bounds, signed and rollback-safe updates and per-site certificate separation — cannot be verified here, and must not be scored as present on the strength of those documents.

risks.title: No code path from the platform reaches a programmable controller, because the capability is absent
preconditions: None. This entry records an absence of capability, verified by an absence of dependency.

evidence.note: Nothing crosses from the platform's side: no command-dispatch surface and no mechanism to write a tag or issue a process command. Emergency stop, interlocks and safety controllers are physically and logically outside this repository.
No library in the dependency tree can speak any industrial protocol; the names appear under the application only as domain vocabulary, enum values, knowledge-base text and interface strings.

existingControls: The cloud-to-controller attack path does not exist because the capability does not exist.
Industrial data enters only through the signed gateway-envelope surface, which is outbound-initiated by the gateway.
controlGaps: This stops being true the moment a protocol client enters the dependency manifest, which is precisely why the preconditions for adding one must be defined before it is added.
acceptanceCriteria: A gate fails the build when a package capable of speaking an industrial protocol enters the dependency manifest without an approved precondition record.
The preconditions for adding one are written down before any such dependency is proposed: direction of initiation, command authorisation, safety interlocking, and what must never be writable.
risks.residualRisk: An absence of capability is the strongest control available and the easiest to lose by accident, in a single dependency addition. It is recorded as a positive control with a gate rather than as a permanent property.

risks.title: Backup, restore and recovery machinery exists and none of it was executed
preconditions: None: the gap is the absence of an executed rehearsal in this programme.

evidence.note: A substantial recovery toolset exists — release manifest and journal, blue-green, migration gates, recovery set and ownership, recovery objectives, backup envelope and retention, uploads archive and restore, and verification — with envelope encryption configured from the environment.
No backup was taken and no restore was performed; a restore rehearsal job exists in continuous integration and S0 does not assert that it passes.

existingControls: The machinery is real and extensive, and a restore rehearsal job exists in the pipeline.
Backup envelopes are encrypted with a configured key and a minimum verified-copy count.
A prior phase found and fixed a defect where backup verification was silently passing, so the failure mode is known to this codebase.
controlGaps: An unexercised restore is a hypothesis; this programme produced no evidence that data can be recovered.
No recovery-point or recovery-time measurement was taken.
acceptanceCriteria: A restore from a production-shaped backup into an isolated environment is executed and the result recorded, including measured recovery point and recovery time.
The uploads and documents volumes are included, not only the database.
The rehearsal is repeated on a schedule, and a failed rehearsal is treated as an incident.
risks.residualRisk: A rehearsal in an isolated environment does not prove recovery under production conditions, with real data volumes and real time pressure; it bounds the unknown rather than removing it. No destructive operation may be performed against production to close this.

risks.title: No incident runbook exists
preconditions: None: the directory does not exist.

evidence.note: The runbook directory does not exist, and the programme requires seven.
Rules of engagement exist for a review, which is the nearest existing artifact and is not an incident runbook.

existingControls: Structured logging, correlation identifiers and an operator console exist, so the raw material an incident needs is present.
An incident rehearsal script exists in the pipeline tooling.
controlGaps: There is no written procedure for the incidents this register makes most likely: a database outage with silent fallback, a suspected gateway compromise, or a credential exposure.
R-34 shows that the one operation an operator would reach for during a gateway incident can report success without acting, and no runbook tells them to verify it.
acceptanceCriteria: A runbook exists for each incident class this register identifies as likely, naming the detection signal, the first action, the verification step and the escalation path.
The gateway-compromise runbook explicitly tells the operator to verify that a revocation took effect, because the current implementation can report otherwise.
Each runbook is rehearsed once and corrected from what the rehearsal reveals.
risks.residualRisk: An unrehearsed runbook is a document, not a capability; the rehearsal criterion is what makes this entry closable, and rehearsals are the part most likely to be deferred.

risks.title: Worker containers receive the whole production environment, so the image-level minimality does not bound the credentials a compromised worker holds
preconditions: Code execution inside a worker container, for example through a compromised base image or a flaw in the worker script's handling of a response.
The production environment file holds the variables the web tier reads; its contents were not read, so which secrets it holds is inferred from the web tier's documented configuration.

evidence.note: The image copies one dependency-free script and says it holds no database credential.
Each worker service declares env_file for the whole production environment file; the new service does the same.
A packaging test asserts the runner and migrator stages copy no scripts at all.

Each worker image contains exactly one dependency-free script: no installed packages, no object-relational mapper, no application code and no database credential, so a worker cannot corrupt state it cannot reach.
The release gate registers each worker's env_file as intended, for the token.
The script itself reads only the worker token chain, the base URL, the interval and the batch size.

existingControls: Each worker reaches the platform through one authenticated request, so the web tier's authorization and audit apply to its work.
The work is leased or idempotent at the web tier, so a retry is safe.
A committed test keeps the packaging boundary from eroding.
Each worker image contains one dependency-free script, no installed packages, no object-relational mapper and no application code (the former positive control, kept as a counter-control).
The workers publish no port, mount no volume and sit on the internal network.
controlGaps: The container environment is the whole file, not the few variables the script reads.
No test asserts that a worker service lists an explicit environment instead of the file.
The former positive control measured image contents, not the run-time environment.
acceptanceCriteria: A gate that fails the build when a worker service in the production compose file declares env_file or lists a variable the worker script does not read.
A test asserts that the image packaging boundary (no application code, no installed packages) still holds.
Worker token rotation is covered by whatever secret-lifecycle work R-49 produces.
risks.residualRisk: An explicit environment bounds what a compromised worker can read, not what it can do with its one credential, and the same pattern in the web tier's own container is out of scope here.

supersedes.title: The worker boundary is deliberately minimal and holds no database credential

revision.reason: The production compose file injects the whole production environment file into every worker container, including the one added since the frozen source, so the image-level minimality recorded as a positive control does not bound the credentials the running process holds. The positive control stays recorded as an existing control.

risks.title: The rate limiter fails closed on an undeclared bucket and audits the refusal
preconditions: None. This entry records a control that is present, and it corrects a claim an earlier document made in the opposite direction.

evidence.note: The corrected section, which replaced an inverted claim taken from a product comment instead of from the limiter itself.

Refuses rather than permits, both in the Redis path and in the in-process fallback, returns a default retry window so a refusal does not advertise an immediate retry, logs at error level and writes an infrastructure audit event naming the bucket and the calling site.

existingControls: Thirty-four actions are registered and kept honest by a committed registry test.
Inventing a new action name would block the route outright and raise an audited error, so it cannot be used to remove a limit.
The in-process fallback is tighter under degradation, never unlimited.
controlGaps: The registry enforces that an action exists, not that it is semantically distinct, which is the gap R-21 sits in.
acceptanceCriteria: The registry test continues to assert that every action used by a route is registered.
A test asserts the refusal on an undeclared action, so the behaviour this entry records cannot regress silently.
risks.residualRisk: The product comments that describe this control still state the opposite, which is tracked as R-27; a reader who trusts the comment will still reach the wrong conclusion until those are corrected.

risks.title: No role can assign organization ownership, and every client-supplied role is clamped
preconditions: None. This entry records a control that is present and load-bearing.

evidence.note: All three places that accept a client-supplied role clamp it, and one of them records that the clamp is a fix for a real prior defect in which an administrator could mint an owner invitation.
No role can assign the owner role, and an administrator cannot even assign administrator.

existingControls: The clamp is applied after a permission check, so both the permission and the target role are validated.
The invitation path validates membership of a role set and then applies the clamp, so the broader set is harmless only because the second check exists.
No route contains a direct role comparison, so there is no second path that could diverge.
controlGaps: The clamp is load-bearing and its removal would silently restore a known defect; the negative tests that would catch that are the subject of R-14.
acceptanceCriteria: A test asserts that no role can assign ownership through any route that accepts a role.
The clamp is covered by the negative-test matrix produced for R-14.
risks.residualRisk: Because ownership cannot be assigned at all, an organization that loses its owner cannot regain one through the platform; that consequence is the policy question in R-15 rather than a defect in this control.

risks.title: The compliance organization-scope helper has a complete fail-closed ladder
preconditions: None. This entry records a control that is present across thirty-five route files.

evidence.note: The organization identity is resolved server-side from active membership rows and never from client input.
Refuses an unverifiable token, a revoked session, an unavailable database, an ambiguous membership and a missing active organization, each with its own status and each logged.

existingControls: An unavailable database produces a refusal rather than a fallback, which is the opposite of the repository fallback in R-32 and shows the correct pattern exists.
An ambiguous membership refuses rather than guessing, unlike the billing resolver in R-11.
controlGaps: The permission is an argument, so the privilege tier is invisible to the classifier — which is R-13, a reporting gap rather than an enforcement one.
acceptanceCriteria: A test exists for each rung of the ladder, so a future change cannot remove one silently.
This helper is used as the reference pattern when R-11 and R-32 are remediated.
risks.residualRisk: The ladder protects the thirty-five compliance route files that use it; the rest of the estate does not, which is the asymmetry R-63 describes.

risks.title: The enterprise-resource surface is the reference implementation of the target failure policy
preconditions: None. This entry records a control that is present across twenty-six route files.

evidence.note: Four gates in order on every route file, with an origin refusal on every write, applied uniformly across a whole module — the shape the rest of the estate does not yet have.
Raises a controlled refusal when the client is unavailable, so no raw database error reaches a caller and no path degrades to process storage.
Carries the organization and the derived capability, resolved server-side.

existingControls: The four-gate chain is uniform, so there is no per-route judgement to get wrong.
Every write is origin-checked, which no other module does.
Financial fields are nulled rather than zeroed when the capability is absent, and a flag tells the client the difference between zero and withheld.
controlGaps: The capability is a derived boolean with no textual signature, so no classifier can see it — which is R-13, and the remediation there should register this capability as its first example.
acceptanceCriteria: The four-gate chain and the controlled refusal are named as the target pattern in the remediation of R-32 and R-36.
The derived capability is the first entry in the capability registry produced for R-13.
risks.residualRisk: A reference implementation inside the same codebase is the strongest argument that the rest of the estate can reach the same standard; it is also evidence that the standard is not currently applied, which is why the risks it contrasts with are scored where they are.

risks.title: There is exactly one mutation transport, because the framework's alternative is unused
preconditions: None. This entry records a structural property that narrows the whole mutation surface.

evidence.note: Zero server actions anywhere in the application, so every state change must pass through an inventoried route handler and no second mutation transport exists.
The mutation surface is therefore exactly the inventoried handlers plus the workers' authenticated requests.

existingControls: The route inventory is a complete enumeration of the mutation surface rather than a sample of it.
There is no transport that bypasses route-level authorization.
controlGaps: The property is maintained by convention; a single server action would silently widen the surface and the inventory would not report it.
acceptanceCriteria: A gate fails the build when a server action is introduced without an explicit decision, because it would widen the mutation surface beyond the inventory.
risks.residualRisk: The property is what makes the route inventory meaningful; losing it would invalidate every count in this register that is derived from the handler set.

risks.title: The session store and the tenant contract both fail closed by construction
preconditions: None. These two entries record controls that are present and are the backbone of the identity and tenancy model.

evidence.locator: the contract and the active check
evidence.note: A missing row, a revoked row, an expired row or an unreachable database are all treated as revoked, and the module is documented as never to be imported from the edge runtime.
Only one state carries an organization identifier, which makes a tenant-scoped query without an established tenant unwritable rather than merely discouraged.

existingControls: The refusal on an unreachable database is the correct direction and is the opposite of the repository fallback in R-32.
The contract's type design removes a whole class of defect rather than guarding against it at each call site.
The screening in R-60 confirmed these two by tracing their callers rather than by reading their names.
controlGaps: The session store's force is undermined by the one sid-less branch described in R-02, which is a branch above it rather than a defect in it.
The contract's guarantee is undermined where a data layer queries without a predicate at all, which is R-08.
acceptanceCriteria: Tests assert the fail-closed behaviour of the session store on each of its four conditions, including an unreachable database.
A test asserts that the tenant contract's ambiguous and unavailable states carry no organization identifier.
risks.residualRisk: Both controls are correct and both are bypassed by a path above them, which is the pattern worth carrying forward: a fail-closed core does not make the system fail closed.

risks.title: Twelve security-control dependencies were traced and confirmed to deny rather than to succeed emptily
preconditions: None. This entry records the outcome of screening twelve sites whose automatic classification was wrong.

evidence.note: All twelve had been classified as an empty success because a rule matched a false or null return; every one is a denial, and most say so in their own comments.
A missing policy denies external egress rather than permitting it.
No database means a closed decision, and the resolver converts unknown usage to a value that forces refusal.

existingControls: The session revocation check, both actor contexts, the login credential lookup, three entitlement reads, the egress policy store, the academy request scope, the candidate retention check and two tenant-context readers all deny when the database is unavailable.
The academy request scope binds its callers in a comment: an empty result must be treated as no access, never as no filter.
The candidate retention check states that an outage is a refusal and never an acceptance, on a public path.
controlGaps: The inventory had been publishing a wrong verdict on the platform's session, tenant, entitlement and egress controls, which is the reporting lesson rather than an enforcement one.
acceptanceCriteria: Each of the twelve has a test asserting that an unavailable database produces a denial rather than an empty success.
The fingerprint-pinned adjudications that record these twelve remain under the deterministic gate, so a code change that alters them fails the build.
risks.residualRisk: These twelve were found only because the residual was screened rather than assumed; the same class of misclassification may exist wherever a rule reads a return value without reading the caller, which is the documented limitation of the instrument.

risks.title: No public handler accepts a tenant, user or role identifier, and every privileged column a public writer sets is hardcoded
preconditions: None. This entry records the outcome of reading all fifty public handlers one by one.

evidence.note: No public handler returns another tenant's data, none accepts a tenant, user or role identifier, and every privileged column a public writer sets is hardcoded; the unsafe category is empty.
The one public handler that creates a user hardcodes the role and the unverified flag, which is the critical control on that route and it is correct.
Public reads are gated on a published-and-public predicate inside the data layer rather than in the route.

existingControls: Every public route file's rate-limit action is registered, and the limiter fails closed on an undeclared one, so no public handler is silently unlimited.
The anti-enumeration posture is real and consistent across four of the five authentication writers.
Published predicates live in the data layer where no route may restate them.
controlGaps: One route contradicts the enumeration posture, which is R-07.
Six handlers are classified as misclassified rather than public, which is R-17.
acceptanceCriteria: A gate asserts that no handler on the public allowlist reads a tenant, user or role identifier from the request.
The allowlist keeps a written justification per entry, as it does now.
risks.residualRisk: This was established by reading fifty handlers at one commit; it is a property of that reading, and only a gate makes it a property of the repository.

risks.title: The gateway envelope is canonicalised and replay-bounded by construction
preconditions: None. This entry records a control that is present on the industrial ingestion surface.

evidence.note: The replay fields are inside the signed set, no model stores key material, and no secret or signature is logged or returned.

evidence.locator: the canonical byte construction and the comparison
evidence.note: Length-prefixed fields in a fixed order rather than a serialisation of caller-supplied objects, compared with a timing-safe comparison.

existingControls: Canonicalising by construction removes the whole class of signature-confusion defects that arise from serialising caller input.
The tenant is a signed field read from the gateway's own record, so a forged envelope cannot claim another organization.
An unresolvable key reference produces a rejection rather than a default.
controlGaps: The signature is only as good as the secret's separation and lifecycle, which is R-49.
acceptanceCriteria: Tests assert the canonical byte order, the timing-safe comparison and the rejection of an unknown algorithm.
A test asserts that an envelope claiming a different organization fails verification.
risks.residualRisk: A correct signature scheme over a shared secret is still a shared-secret scheme; this entry records the quality of the construction, not the strength of the identity, which is R-49.

risks.title: There is no central authorization choke point for the application interface
preconditions: None: the middleware matcher excludes the interface prefix and every dotted path, so the property holds for every request.

evidence.note: Five hundred and seventy-two handlers are five hundred and seventy-two independent enforcement decisions, and the repository's answer to that risk is a lexical inventory that cannot prove any handler's enforcement is reached on every branch.
The inventory indexes the surface; it is an index, never an isolation proof.
Excludes the interface prefix and any path containing a dot, so neither authentication nor the content policy reaches those requests.

existingControls: Every handler must prove authorization evidence in its own source or be classified unknown, and unknown fails readiness.
The enterprise-resource module shows a uniform four-gate chain is achievable across a whole module.
There is only one mutation transport, so the surface is at least completely enumerable.
No handler is currently classified unknown.
controlGaps: A new handler that forgets its gate is caught only by a lexical classifier that cannot see past the route file, so the depth of the check does not match the depth of the risk.
Static assets served from inside the public directory receive neither authorization nor a content policy, which is the surface R-22 writes to.
The classifier's own limitations are the subject of R-13, so the compensating control for this architectural choice is itself a known assurance gap.
acceptanceCriteria: A decision is recorded on whether a shared enforcement wrapper is adopted for the interface, with the enterprise-resource chain as the candidate pattern, because retrofitting it touches every handler.
Until then, the classifier is strengthened per R-13 so that a handler without a reached gate cannot pass as classified.
A response-header policy covers the static upload path, which middleware does not reach.
risks.residualRisk: A central wrapper concentrates the decision and therefore concentrates the failure: a defect in it would affect every handler at once. That is a better trade than five hundred and seventy-two independent decisions, and it is still a trade, which is why the first criterion is a recorded decision rather than an implementation.

risks.title: Five security-relevant surfaces were declared out of scope in the source phase and remain unexamined
preconditions: None: the gap is that these five were never read, so nothing is known about them in either direction.

evidence.note: The one hundred and thirty-five platform-administrative handlers were not re-audited and are explicitly not asserted correct, only not contradicted.
Classified as a webhook; the signature verification was not read and is explicitly deferred.
Present; its scope and coverage were not established.
Present and not inspected in the source phase.
The document authorization path; the signed-token lifetime and the re-authorization behaviour on download were not verified.

existingControls: Each of the five is recorded as unexamined rather than assumed sound, which is why they appear here at all.
The inventory reports no unauthenticated webhook, which is a lexical result rather than a reading of the signature check.
The document volume is outside the public directory and is reached only through an authorizing path.
controlGaps: A single-sign-on implementation is an authentication surface and nothing is known about it.
The platform-administrative tier is the largest privileged classification in the inventory and has never been audited handler by handler.
A webhook signature check is the only thing standing between a payment provider's identity and an unauthenticated write.
acceptanceCriteria: Each of the five is examined and its result recorded, with the webhook signature check and the platform-administrative tier taken first because they carry the most authority.
Any finding is added to this register with its own risk entry rather than appended to this one.
This entry is closed only when all five have been read, not when a subset has.
risks.residualRisk: THE CONFIDENCE ON THIS ENTRY IS LOW AND THE SCORE IS THEREFORE THE LEAST RELIABLE IN THE REGISTER. It is an estimate of the risk of not knowing, derived from what these surfaces are rather than from what they contain, and it may move sharply in either direction once they are read.

risks.title: An archived nightly report is shown at the organization's full breadth, so a lower-privileged reader sees financial and all-site data that the live dashboard refuses
preconditions: The reader holds the platform administrator capability and an active membership of the organization, with an organization role that lacks the financial axis (every role but OWNER) or holds a subset of sites.
At least one stored report exists. The runner is documented as not started by the deploy, so the archive holds rows only after the runner is activated or a platform administrator triggers a pass.
That a platform administrator stays within an organization role is a design assumption; no run-time evidence in this programme confirms or refutes it.

The nightly pass also freezes a ranked list of the next day's priorities into its own column of the report row, built under the same synthetic OWNER scope, which now also holds the customers axis and every active site; the list names customers, work items, approvals and open alerts without regard to the reader.

evidence.note: The stored snapshot is rendered through the shared view with no authority or site check; only the organization is taken from the scope. The archive list returns envelopes only and there is no download or export route.

The list is computed in the generating pass from the synthetic scope and stored next to the snapshot.

risks.title: The customer project panel returns summed project cost to ADMIN, who is refused cost figures on every ERP surface
preconditions: The caller is an ADMIN of the organization, which holds view_erp and view_customers but not view_erp_compensation.
At least one project is linked to a customer and has cost rows.

No authoritative document says whether a customer-level cost aggregate is outside the compensation gate. The behaviour (the route returns recordedCost to an ADMIN) is confirmed in code; whether it is wanted is undecided and is recorded in policy.

evidence.note: The route requires view_customers and view_erp and does not require view_erp_compensation.
The response carries recordedCost, summed from the cost ledger per currency, for any caller the route admits.
The ERP layer nulls budget and actual cost for everyone without the compensation permission.
ADMIN holds view_erp; only OWNER holds view_erp_compensation.

existingControls: The query is filtered by the server-resolved organization and by the customer's own projects.
Only OWNER and ADMIN reach the route; both are privileged roles of the same organization.
controlGaps: The cost aggregate is not gated on the compensation permission.
Linking a project to a customer discloses project granularity to the customer-management role, limited by the need for manage_erp.
No test asserts either behaviour: neither that an ADMIN does not receive recordedCost nor that the aggregate is the only cost the route returns.
acceptanceCriteria: If the owner decides that the recorded-cost total is an ERP compensation figure: a test asserts that the customer project route called as an ADMIN returns recordedCost as absent or null, and a test asserts that the same route called as an OWNER returns the figures.

If the owner decides that the recorded-cost total is a customer-level aggregate outside the compensation gate: the difference from the ERP surfaces is written into the customer feature documentation, a test asserts that the route returns nothing finer than one amount per currency (no per-project cost), and a test asserts that every role without view_erp, including MANAGER, receives no project data and no recordedCost.
risks.residualRisk: Gating the aggregate leaves the project list itself visible to anyone with view_erp, which is intended. Whether a customer-level cost view should exist at all for ADMIN is an owner decision: both outcomes are recorded in policy with their own testable criteria, and neither is chosen here.

policy.question: Is the per-currency recorded-cost total on a customer an ERP compensation figure that only holders of view_erp_compensation (OWNER) may read, or a customer-level aggregate that holders of view_erp (OWNER and ADMIN) may read?

risks.title: The nightly-report entrypoint accepts any of three bearer tokens, is public with no origin check or rate limit, and returns other tenants' organization ids
preconditions: The caller holds one of EXECUTIVE_REPORT_WORKER_TOKEN, METERING_WORKER_TOKEN or METRICS_TOKEN, or a platform-administrator session.
The metrics token is the one most likely to be held by a third-party scraper; whether it is, and how strong any of the three tokens is, was not observed.

evidence.note: A single catch-all location proxies every path; no allow-list or rate limit applies to this route.

evidence.locator: the worker guard performs the checks its registration vouches for
evidence.note: The test locks the accept-all chain by asserting that the guard source names all three variables.
The whole pass report is returned, and the route imports no origin or rate-limit helper.
Every configured token among three is compared and any match opens the door; the module comment says setting the dedicated variable closes the others, which the code does not do.
Failures, undelivered entries and the pagination cursor carry organization ids of tenants other than the caller's.

existingControls: The comparison is constant-time, and with no token configured and no administrator session the endpoint answers 401.
The pass is bounded to 200 organizations per request, leased and idempotent, and the notification carries no figures.
The session cookies are strict or lax, so a cross-site POST does not carry them.
controlGaps: Three credentials with different intended blast radii open the same door.
The response is not reduced to counts for a token caller, and paging with the returned cursor enumerates every organization id.
The sibling cookie-authenticated writes refuse an untrusted Origin; this one does not.
No per-credential rate limit protects the token comparison.
acceptanceCriteria: A test asserts that, with the dedicated token configured, the metering token and the metrics token are refused.
A test asserts that the token-path response contains no organization id.
A test asserts that the entrypoint refuses an untrusted Origin on the session path.
risks.residualRisk: A dedicated token still travels in the environment of the runner and of the web tier; token strength and rotation are outside this entry (R-49), and the entrypoint remains an internet-facing route whose only barrier is that token.

risks.title: The nightly-report path can freeze, announce or report something other than what happened: a default-zone freeze, a transient site-read failure stored as a FORBIDDEN section, announced-but-undelivered, an outage shown as a normal state, and skipped or colliding business days
preconditions: A failure of the batched settings read or of the single site read during a pass, or of the claim release, or an outage of the database while the runner polls; or an organization administrator changing the reporting zone or cutoff; or a night that passes with no pass running.
The runner is documented as not started by the deploy; until it runs, the archive is empty.

evidence.note: An unreadable archive renders as a missing report.
An existing report is found by organization and date label only; nothing regenerates a stored night and no caller supplies a correction.
The release of a claim is discarded and its failure swallowed; an absent client yields an empty pass; a failed claim is not listed as undelivered.
An unreadable site list is returned as an empty list, which the industrial section answers as FORBIDDEN (no site granted) and the report stores.
Every id starts as the default and stays so when the batched query throws.

existingControls: Each stored report names the zone and cutoff it used.
The next poll retries an unreported night within the same day.
The archive list page distinguishes an unreadable archive from an empty one.
controlGaps: A failed batched read is indistinguishable from an absent row.
A failed site read is indistinguishable from an organization with no site, and is stored with a permission reason.
A failed claim release is neither logged, retried nor persisted.
No signal separates no-database from nothing-to-do on the worker path or the detail page.
The lookup ignores the zone and cutoff, and each pass targets only the last completed day.
acceptanceCriteria: A test asserts that a failed batched settings read writes no report.
A test asserts that a failed site read writes no FORBIDDEN industrial section and leaves the night open for a later pass.
A test asserts that a failed claim release is reported by the pass and retried by a later pass.
A test asserts that a pass with no database does not look like a held lease and that the detail page shows an unavailable state for an unreadable archive.
A test asserts that a night missed entirely is reported by a later pass and that a zone change cannot reuse a stored label for a different window.
risks.residualRisk: Fixing the four paths does not make a stored report correctable by itself: the correction path exists in the library and no caller issues it, which is a product decision.

evidence.note: Nothing records who opened a report.

risks.title: Linking a project to a customer is check-then-write: concurrent links can overwrite each other while both audit rows claim success
preconditions: Two members holding manage_customers and manage_erp link the same project to different customers at nearly the same time, or a project is deleted between the check and the update.
The database runs at its default isolation level.

evidence.note: The project is read once; the update filters by id and organization only and does not check the row count; the audit event follows unconditionally.

existingControls: Both foreign keys are composite, so a link cannot cross organizations for a row that has an organization.
The transaction keeps the read, the update and the audit together.
controlGaps: The update has no precondition on the partyId that was read and does not repeat the deletedAt filter.
The audit event is written whatever the update changed.
acceptanceCriteria: A test asserts that a link whose precondition no longer holds changes nothing and writes no success audit event.
A test asserts that two concurrent links of one project leave exactly one link and exactly one matching audit event.
risks.residualRisk: A conditional update fixes this path only; any other writer of ErpProject.partyId would need the same precondition.

risks.title: Customer name uniqueness is enforced only by a read before the insert, so concurrent creates or a double submit can store duplicates
preconditions: Two requests creating or renaming customers to the same name in the same organization run concurrently, for example a double submit of the creation form.

evidence.note: The only unique index is on organization and id; none covers the name.
A case-insensitive read decides uniqueness inside the transaction; the insert follows.

existingControls: The same-name read refuses the ordinary sequential duplicate with a stated conflict.

controlGaps: No database constraint backs the rule, so a race stores two active customers with one name.
acceptanceCriteria: A test asserts that two concurrent creates of one name store exactly one active customer.
risks.residualRisk: A partial unique index on the lower-cased active name changes existing rows only if duplicates already exist; the migration needs a check for them first.

risks.title: The customer and project-link surface skips the platform-administrator gate that all ERP routes apply, so an organization owner or administrator who is not a platform admin reads ERP project data and changes a project's customer
preconditions: The caller is an OWNER or ADMIN of an organization (view_customers, view_erp and manage_erp) whose account does not hold the platform admin capability.
The organization has at least one project, and for a write the caller also holds manage_customers.

Whether tenant owners should reach ERP-derived data without the platform capability is undecided (see policy). The repository's reference behaviour (27 ERP route files, the ERP page scope and the executive scope) requires the capability, while the customer feature documentation grants organization permissions only.

evidence.note: The reference: all 27 ERP route files refuse a caller without the platform capability before the organization permission is checked.
Both handlers resolve the active organization and check organization permissions only; neither reads the platform identity or the platform capability.
The customer pages gate project data on the organization permission only.
The write changes ErpProject.partyId and the list offers the organization's ERP projects.
The executive surface applies the same two layers.

existingControls: The organization is the server-resolved active selection and every query filters by it, so another tenant's data is not reachable.
The customer-to-project foreign key is composite (with the null-organization caveat recorded on R-09).
Reading and writing still need organization permissions and a trusted origin on writes.
controlGaps: The platform capability that gates every ERP route is absent from the customer and project-link routes and pages.
No test asserts either behaviour: neither that a caller who lacks the platform capability is refused by the customer project routes nor that the roles without view_erp are.
acceptanceCriteria: If the owner decides that the platform-administrator capability is required on the customer surface: the customer routes and pages that read or write project data apply the same two layers as the ERP routes (getCurrentUser and can(user.role, "admin") before the organization permission), a test asserts that an OWNER or ADMIN who lacks the platform capability is refused by every customer route that reads or writes project data, and a test asserts that the customer pages do not render project data for such a caller.

If the owner decides that tenant OWNER and ADMIN may use the customer surface without the platform capability: the difference from the ERP routes is stated in the customer feature documentation, the project data a caller may read or change is limited to the fields the owner names, a test asserts that every role without view_erp (and without manage_erp for the link) is refused by the customer project routes, and a test asserts that no ERP route becomes reachable through the customer surface.
risks.residualRisk: Adding the gate makes the customer feature unavailable to tenant owners who are not platform admins, which may be the opposite of the feature's purpose; keeping the difference needs its own documentation and tests. The fix and the product decision cannot be separated, and both outcomes are recorded in policy without choosing one.
